title: Distribution days, drawn
hook: A record high in October 2007. Then the warnings piled up.
takeaway: A distribution day is a session where an index closes down 0.2% or more on higher volume than the day before; O'Neil's school reads it as big funds selling. Count them over the last 25 sessions: four or five in about a month is a warning. In 2007 the S&P 500 closed at a record on October 9 with one on the count; eight trading days later there were five, and eight by November 7. Five months later the index was down 19%, and 57% by March 2009. It's a warning, not a forecast.
learn: A distribution day is a day the index closes down 0.2% or more on higher volume than the day before.
Count them over the last 25 trading days; four or five in about a month is a warning sign.
In 2007 the S&P 500 went from a record close with one distribution day to eight within a month, then fell 19% by March 2008.
The count is a warning, not a forecast: when it piles up, be careful with new buys.

props.label: How to count them
props.sub: A day drops off after 25 sessions, or if the index rallies 5% above it.

captions: Count them over the last 25 trading days.
O'Neil: four or five in a month spells trouble.
Here's the S&P 500 in 2007. Watch the count.
On October 9 it closed at a record. Count: one.
Eight trading days later, the count was five.
By November 7 it hit eight. Prices kept slipping.
By March 2008 the S&P 500 was down 19%.
A year later it was down 57%.

props.text: When the count [[piles up]], go easy on new buys.
props.sub: A warning, not a forecast: some counts fade without a fall.
